fact.thing: extra tax from using the last purchase price instead of the average cost
fact.box: Non-registered crypto holdings, Ontario resident, 2026 taxable income $58,523 to $94,907
fact.claim: For identical properties, the CRA says your cost per unit (ACB) is the total cost of all your purchases divided by the number of units you own. Not your last purchase price. Worked example: buy 3 coins at $9,000, $7,000 and $5,000, for an average cost of $7,000 each. Then sell all 3 for $10,000 each. The correct gain is $9,000, but using the $5,000 last price makes it $15,000. fact.thing: FHSA lifetime contribution limit
fact.box: FHSA to RRSP or RRIF (direct transfer)
fact.claim: You can put at most $40,000 into an FHSA over your lifetime, and no more than $8,000 in the year you open your first one. If you never buy a home, you can move the money directly into your RRSP or RRIF by the end of your maximum participation period, which is the earliest of 15 years after you open the account, the year you turn 71, or the year after your first qualifying withdrawal. Generally, a direct transfer does not use up your unused RRSP deduction room and has no immediate tax. This only works as a direct transfer with no excess FHSA amount: if you withdraw the cash and then put it into your RRSP, the withdrawal is taxed and counts as a new RRSP contribution.

fact.thing: tax refund on a $5,000 RRSP contribution at the 29.65% combined federal + Ontario rate
fact.box: RRSP (2026 tax year, Ontario resident on Dec 31, 2026)
fact.claim: In 2026, taxable income from $58,523.01 to $107,785 is taxed at 20.5% federal plus 9.15% Ontario, for a combined marginal rate of 29.65%. If your taxable income is in that range both before and after the deduction, a $5,000 RRSP deduction lowers your tax by about $1,483. Other brackets get different amounts: about $1,158 at 23.15% (from $53,891.01 to $58,523), and Ontario's surtax and health premium can change the result for some incomes. The CRA's rule says the 2026 contribution year ends on the 60th day of 2027, which is Monday, March 1, 2027. The CRA has not posted that date on its own pages yet, and money contributed after that date can't be deducted on your 2026 return.

fact.thing: repeated failure to report income penalty
fact.box: Your T1 income tax return (CRA)
fact.claim: Trading one crypto-asset for another type of crypto-asset can count as a disposition, so you have to report it on your return. If you leave out $500 or more on your 2025 return and also left out income on your 2022, 2023 or 2024 return, the CRA can charge a penalty. The penalty is whichever is less: 10% of the amount you failed to report (federal and provincial or territorial), or 50% of the understated tax minus any tax withheld on that amount. One missed swap does not trigger it alone, because it only applies to a repeated failure. Budget 2024 said Canada would bring in the Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework effective as of 2026, with exchanges of information beginning in 2027, pending legislation.

fact.thing: calendar days before and after the sale in the superficial loss window

fact.claim: If you sell crypto at a loss, the CRA treats it as a superficial loss when you, or a person affiliated with you such as a spouse, buy the same or identical property in the period from 30 calendar days before the sale to 30 calendar days after it, and you still own it 30 days after the sale. fact.thing: CRA late-filing penalty
fact.box: Personal income tax return (T1)
fact.claim: If you owe tax and the CRA gets your return after the due date, it charges 5% of the balance owing. The deadline is April 30, or the next business day if April 30 falls on a weekend or holiday. Filing on time avoids this penalty even if you can't pay yet. fact.thing: tax refunded on a $10,000 capital loss carried back
fact.box: Taxable (non-registered) account, past 3 years' returns via Form T1A
fact.claim: You can use a net capital loss to cut your taxable capital gains in any of the three previous years, or carry it forward with no time limit. To carry it back you file Form T1A, and you don't amend the old return. Half of the loss counts (the 50% inclusion rate), and it can only offset capital gains, not wages or other income. For an Ontario resident earning just over $58,523, that half is taxed at a combined 29.65%, so a $10,000 loss gets back about $1,483 of tax paid on earlier gains. This is an example: the real refund depends on your tax rate in the year the gain was taxed.
